idiom_name: #[derive(PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)] plus std::ops traits and blanket-impl-free families
implementation_notes: Rust splits the family in two: comparison operators come from PartialEq/Eq and PartialOrd/Ord, which #[derive] generates member-wise in declaration order (exactly like C++20's defaulted <=>), and arithmetic operators come from the std::ops traits (Add, Sub, Neg, Index, ...), whose impls must be written per type. The C++ trick's 'one definition for the whole family' has no direct analogue because coherence forbids a blanket impl such as impl<T: MyTrait> Add for T (E0210: the type parameter is not covered by a local type), so families are covered by a declarative macro that emits the impls, by a derive macro from a crate such as derive_more, or by generic functions that take the operation as a trait bound. Derive the comparison traits by default, implement std::ops only where operator syntax is genuinely wanted, and remember that Ord requires Eq + PartialOrd and a total order.
pitfalls: Derived PartialOrd/Ord compare fields in declaration order, so reordering fields silently changes comparison semantics; a manual impl must keep a == b equivalent to partial_cmp() == Some(Ordering::Equal).
You cannot write one blanket impl<T: MyTrait> Add for T (or PartialEq for a type parameter) - coherence (E0210/E0117) rejects it, so family-wide operators need a macro or generic functions instead.
Operator traits take operands by value: generic code that must reuse values needs impls for &T or explicit clones, otherwise the operator consumes the operand.
